text:
To understand how a refrigerator maintains its cold interior, we must first recognize that it is not a simple box of ice; rather, it is a closed-loop system of thermodynamics. The magic of a refrigerator lies in the controlled movement of heat. When we place food inside, we are essentially creating a small environment that needs to stay cool to prevent bacterial growth. To achieve this, the refrigerator relies on a cycle that draws heat from the inside and rejects it to the outside. This process requires a series of key components working in unison.

The journey begins with the **compressor**, often the most visible part of the system. Imagine the compressor as a muscular pump. As the compressor runs, it compresses a low-pressure gas of refrigerant, causing its temperature to rise significantly. This high-pressure, hot gas is then sent to the next component. The **condenser**, located on the back or side of the refrigerator, acts as the heat sink. As the hot gas travels through the condenser coils, it releases its excess heat into the surrounding room. This is where the heat we feel from the refrigerator is actually being dumped into the walls and air of our living space. The condenser doesn't cool the food; it cools the refrigerant itself.
